opus-5.5.text:
Ha, yeah. I think it started half as a joke, but the more I thought about it, the more it actually fit.

When Klopp arrived at Liverpool, everyone remembered Mourinho calling himself "the special one," and Klopp said, "I'm the normal one." I really liked that, because in our field there's a lot of pressure to be "special," to be the genius, to have the one big idea that changes everything. Especially in AI right now, there's this whole narrative around a few superstar figures.

But honestly, when I look at myself, I don't feel like that kind of person. I came up through a pretty normal path. I wasn't some prodigy who knew exactly what I wanted to do at fifteen. A lot of what I've done came from working with great people, being in the right environment, and just putting in steady effort, trying things, failing, trying again.

And what I admire about Klopp isn't only the humility. It's that "normal" doesn't mean mediocre. He built teams with enormous intensity and real belief, but the foundation was the collective: the culture, the people, the energy in the room. That's very close to how I think about research. Good research is rarely one lone genius. It's a group of people who trust each other, who are willing to take risks together, and who keep a sense of fun even when things aren't working.

So for me, being "the normal one" is a reminder to stay grounded, to not take myself too seriously, and to focus on building the right environment for people to do great work, rather than trying to perform being special. I think that's healthier, and honestly, in the long run, I think it's also more effective.

r001.rationale: The response discusses Klopp’s “normal one” description and collective team culture, but does not explain a battery metaphor or say Klopp uses his passion and energy to energize teammates.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, you know, when Klopp first came to Liverpool, the press asked him what he'd call himself, since Mourinho had already famously called himself "the special one." And Klopp just said, "I'm the normal one." And I always loved that, because I think it's actually a very confident thing to say. He wasn't being falsely modest. He was saying: I don't need a label, I just want to do the work, and the work will speak for itself.

I identify with that because, honestly, I don't think I'm a genius or anything like that. I was a pretty normal student. I didn't win math olympiads as a kid. When I was doing my PhD, there were people around me who were clearly much faster, much sharper at certain things. And in this field right now there's a lot of this mythology, right? Everyone wants to be the chosen one, the person who had the one brilliant idea that changed everything. But most of research isn't like that. Most of it is showing up every day, running experiments that fail, reading papers carefully, and being honest about what you actually found.

And there's a second part of Klopp's philosophy that I really connect to, which is the way he thinks about teams. He believes that a group of good, normal, committed people who trust each other can beat a team of individual superstars. I think that's true in research too. The best things I've been part of, like ResNeXt, or ConvNeXt, or later the work with students at NYU, those were never one person's idea. They came from a group arguing, iterating, being willing to try something a bit unfashionable. I'd much rather be the person who creates that kind of environment than the person who gets called "special."

So being "the normal one" to me is kind of a relief. It takes the pressure off. You don't have to be a genius. You just have to be curious, persistent, and a decent teammate. And I think that's actually a more sustainable way to do this for a long time.

astra-6.text:
I relate to that phrase because I don’t see myself as someone with an extraordinary gift who was always destined to do this. I’m curious, I enjoy the work, and I’ve had opportunities to learn from people around me. That feels like a very normal way to grow.

You can be ambitious and take your work seriously without thinking you’re special. To me, being “the normal one” means staying grounded, recognizing how much you depend on other people, and continuing to learn.

sol-6.1.text: I think it’s the idea that you don’t have to see yourself as someone special to do meaningful work. You can be a normal person who is curious, works hard, and is lucky enough to work with great people. That resonates with how I see myself. Being introduced through your achievements can make your path sound inevitable, but from the inside, you’re just figuring things out, making mistakes, and learning as you go.
